title: Feinberg v. Pfeiffer Co.
summary: Past work did not supply bargained-for consideration for the pension; retirement induced by the promise supported enforcement through reliance.
notes:
Court: St. Louis Court of Appeals, Missouri (1959).

The same entry combines both assigned excerpts without treating the consideration rejection as the case’s ultimate outcome. Past services and past consideration, reliance on a later promise, and a later medical condition play different roles.

sections.Parties: Feinberg, a longtime employee, sued Pfeiffer Company for pension payments promised in a board resolution.
sections.Material Facts: After many years of service, Feinberg received a salary increase and the right to retire at any time with $200 per month for life. She was not required to work for a further fixed period. She retired about eighteen months later, at age fifty-seven, in reliance on the pension. The company paid until it later attempted to reduce the amount. By that time she was older and less able to obtain new work.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment for $5,100 in unpaid installments. The Missouri appellate decision is divided between an initial consideration excerpt and a later reliance excerpt. The court affirmed the judgment on the reliance ground.
sections.Issue: Were past services or voluntary continued work consideration for the pension, and could retirement induced by the assurance supply a different basis of enforcement?
sections.Holding: Past services were not bargained for in exchange for the later promise, and future service was not required by its terms. Retirement in reliance on the pension made the promise enforceable under the court’s promissory-estoppel analysis.
sections.Reasoning: The resolution’s operation permitted immediate retirement, so subsequent service cannot be inserted as a condition that the board never demanded. The later excerpt focuses on the employee’s induced choice to leave work and the difficulty of reversing that choice after years had passed. Subsequent illness was not the act of reliance: the promise induced retirement. The notes’ Hayes comparison asks what changes if the employee had already decided to retire before receiving the pension assurance.
